Learning Objectives & Big Picture

This lecture connects the posterior extensor compartment to radial nerve course, dorsal cutaneous innervation, radial/ulnar arterial routes, the anatomical snuffbox, and injury localization. Its primary organizing principle is structure → function → lesion → deficit.

  1. Identify posterior forearm muscles, layers, actions, attachments, and nerve supply.
  2. Trace the radial nerve and its cutaneous, superficial, deep, and posterior interosseous branches; predict common injuries.
  3. Map posterior forearm and dorsal hand sensation, including reliable examination sites.
  4. Trace arterial supply and venous return.
  5. Describe snuffbox boundaries, contents, and scaphoid injury implications.
  6. Explain lateral epicondylitis, mallet finger, and localization of major brachial plexus lesions.
  7. Recognize key structures on supplied imaging and anatomy figures.
MUST KNOW: Most posterior forearm muscles extend the wrist/digits or supinate the forearm. The radial nerve supplies the compartment, but lesion deficits depend on where branches departed before injury.

1. Osteology and wrist map

Major landmarks

  • Lateral supracondylar ridge: brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus proximal origins.
  • Lateral epicondyle: common extensor tendon origin.
  • Radius: head with capitulum and radial notch; neck; radial tuberosity for biceps; distal styloid.
  • Ulna: olecranon, coronoid process, ulnar tuberosity for brachialis.
  • Hand: eight carpals, five metacarpals, fourteen phalanges; thumb has proximal/distal phalanges only.
  • Radiocarpal joint: distal radius/articular disc proximally; scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum distally. The ulna does not directly participate in the wrist joint.
CLINICAL CONNECTION: Distal radial carpal relationships help orient fracture and wrist pain imaging. Know the anatomy before interpreting a view.

2. Posterior forearm: compartments and muscle actions

The posterior compartment has superficial and deep layers. Superficial muscles receive radial nerve or deep radial branch innervation; the deep group receives deep radial branch/posterior interosseous nerve supply.

Superficial layer: learn the functional group

MuscleProximal → distal attachmentNerveAction / testing
BrachioradialisLateral supracondylar ridge → distal radiusRadialElbow flexion maximal in mid-pronation; resist elbow flexion in neutral forearm.
ECRLSupracondylar ridge → base metacarpal 2RadialWrist extension + radial deviation.
ECRBLateral epicondyle → base metacarpal 3Deep radial branchWrist extension + radial deviation.
Extensor digitorumCommon extensor tendon → extensor expansions digits 2–5Deep radial branch (lecture slides); posterior interosseous (handout)Primarily MCP extension, secondarily IP extension.
Extensor digiti minimiLateral epicondyle → expansion digit 5Deep radial branch (slides); posterior interosseous (handout)Independent little-finger extension.
ECULateral epicondyle → base metacarpal 5Deep radial branch (slides); posterior interosseous (handout)Wrist extension + ulnar deviation.

Source distinction: the slides name the deep radial branch for several superficial extensors, while the accompanying handout labels their innervation posterior interosseous. Both names are preserved here; their continuity through supinator explains the variation in descriptions.

Mechanism: ECRL/ECRB extend and radially deviate the wrist; ECU extends and ulnarly deviates. Coordinated flexor + extensor action produces pure deviation by canceling opposite flexion/extension components.

Deep layer

MuscleInsertions / anatomyNerveAction
SupinatorUlna/lateral epicondyle → proximal radiusDeep radial branchRotates radius to turn palm anteriorly.
APLUlna/radius/interosseous membrane → metacarpal 1Posterior interosseousThumb abduction and CMC extension.
EPBRadius/interosseous membrane → thumb proximal phalanxPosterior interosseousThumb MCP extension.
EPLUlna/interosseous membrane → thumb distal phalanxPosterior interosseousThumb IP extension (also MCP/CMC).
Extensor indicisUlna/interosseous membrane → digit 2 expansionPosterior interosseousIndependent index extension.
COMMON CONFUSION: EPB extends at the thumb MCP; EPL reaches the distal phalanx and extends the IP joint; APL abducts the thumb at its CMC articulation.

3. Extensor retinaculum, dorsal hood, and injuries

Extensor retinaculum: thickened deep fascia forms osseofibrous passages against distal radius/ulna; it holds tendons close to bone and prevents bowstringing. Synovial sheaths reduce friction; tenosynovitis involves inflammation of tendon/sheath.

Dorsal hood/expansion: extensor digitorum joins the dorsal expansion with lumbricals and interossei. The intrinsic hand muscles use this expansion to permit the characteristic combination of MCP flexion with PIP/DIP extension.

Two clinical presentations

Lateral epicondylitis (“tennis elbow”)

Repetitive loading of superficial extensors at the common tendon causes lateral elbow pain; the slides emphasize a tendinosis / non-inflammatory degeneration concept. Treatment discussed: activity changes, bracing, analgesics, PT; anti-inflammatory treatment is controversial.

Mallet finger

Sudden forced DIP flexion while attempting extension disrupts the distal extensor insertion, sometimes avulsing bone. The patient cannot actively extend the DIP joint. Slides list splinting and surgery as treatment possibilities.

Source discrepancy: The supplementary handout calls lateral epicondylitis an inflammatory periosteal strain, while the primary slides specifically frame it as tendinosis and state anti-inflammatory treatment is controversial. The notes retain the distinction rather than silently resolving it.

4. Anatomical snuffbox & scaphoid

The snuffbox is a triangular hollow on the dorsolateral wrist when the thumb is extended.

  • Lateral/anterior border: APL and EPB tendons.
  • Medial/posterior border: EPL tendon.
  • Floor: scaphoid and trapezium.
  • Radial artery passes through the floor; superficial radial sensory nerve crosses superficial to it.
  • Palpable nearby: radial styloid and base of first metacarpal.
EXAM TRAP / CLINICAL: FOOSH + snuffbox tenderness → suspect scaphoid fracture. Blood supply largely enters distally and travels retrograde, so a proximal scaphoid segment is at risk of avascular necrosis when fractured.

5. Radial nerve: trace before you localize

Posterior cord (C5–T1) → radial nerve → arm radial groove with profunda brachii artery → cubital fossa between brachialis and brachioradialis → superficial sensory and deep motor branches.

Branch-level logic

StructureCourse / functionWhat lesion suggests
Posterior antebrachial cutaneous n.Branches in arm; posterior forearm sensationMore distal forearm injury can spare posterior forearm sensation.
Radial nerve properTriceps branches in arm; brachioradialis/ECRL in proximal forearmHigh lesion can affect elbow, wrist, digital extension and cutaneous sensation.
Superficial radial n.Sensory only; dorsolateral hand and first dorsal web spaceSensory change without extensor paralysis.
Deep radial branchMotor; pierces supinator, supplies ECRB, superficial extensors, supinatorWrist/finger extension or supination impairment without dorsal hand skin sensory loss.
Posterior interosseous n.Deep radial branch after emerging from supinator; supplies APL, EPB, EPL, extensor indicisDistal thumb/finger extension weakness; no first web-space sensory loss.
COMMON CONFUSION: Posterior interosseous nerve is motor in this lecture; first dorsal web-space sensation tests the superficial radial nerve. Both are branches of the radial nerve, but an isolated motor lesion need not cause skin numbness.
FIRST AID CONNECTION: Localize radial nerve lesions by asking whether triceps, wrist extensors, finger extensors and first dorsal web space sensation are affected. The more proximal the lesion, the more branches may be involved.

6. Posterior forearm, dorsal hand, and dermatomes

  • Posterior antebrachial cutaneous: radial nerve branch in arm → posterior forearm.
  • Lateral antebrachial cutaneous: continuation of musculocutaneous → lateral forearm.
  • Medial antebrachial cutaneous: medial cord → medial forearm.
  • Superficial radial: dorsolateral hand and first dorsal web space.
  • Dorsal ulnar branches: medial dorsal hand and little finger region.
  • Median digital branches: dorsal distal tips/nail beds of lateral digits; examine these separately from proximal dorsal hand.
MUST KNOW: dermatome vs peripheral nerve territory

C6 thumb; C7 digit 3; C8 digit 5. These identify roots, while the first dorsal web space is used for a radial peripheral nerve sensory exam. Do not treat them as interchangeable maps.

Retrieval checkpoint: Why may a radial injury below the elbow leave posterior forearm sensation intact? Because its posterior antebrachial cutaneous branch already left the nerve in the arm.

7. Posterior forearm arteries and dorsal venous return

Brachial artery bifurcates at the cubital fossa into radial and ulnar arteries. Ulnar artery → common interosseous → anterior/posterior interosseous arteries. The posterior interosseous artery runs between extensor layers alongside the posterior interosseous nerve.

High-yield route: radial artery → anatomical snuffbox → between heads of first dorsal interosseous → palm → anastomosis with deep ulnar branch → deep palmar arch.

Superficial veins: dorsal venous network of hand → lateral cephalic and medial basilic veins. The handout traces cephalic through the deltopectoral groove to axillary vein; basilic passes deep through brachial fascia and joins brachial veins.

8. Localize radial nerve and brachial plexus injuries

Mid-humeral shaft lesion

The nerve is vulnerable in the radial groove. The lecture handout associates injury with weakness in triceps/brachioradialis/supinator/wrist extensors and wrist drop, plus possible posterior forearm/dorsoradial hand sensory changes. Extent depends on lesion location and branching.

Assess distal pulses and capillary refill in traumatic arm injury; the lecture explicitly asks for vascular examination.

Lesion regionExpected distinguishing clues
Axilla / high radialBroad motor extensor deficits, potentially triceps and cutaneous territories.
Radial groove / humeral shaftWrist drop, possible radial skin sensory deficits; evaluate triceps branch variability.
Deep radial or PIN near supinatorMotor-predominant finger/thumb extension weakness with intact superficial radial cutaneous sensation.
Superficial radial branchFirst dorsal web-space sensory changes without wrist drop.
Upper trunk (C5–C6) / Erb-DuchenneShoulder adduction/internal rotation, extended elbow, pronated forearm, flexed wrist: “waiter's tip.”
Lower trunk (C8–T1) / KlumpkeIntrinsic hand weakness / claw hand; typically traction on abducted upper limb.
EXAM TRAP: A brachial plexus lesion typically spans more than one terminal nerve's territory. A first web-space-only sensory problem points toward superficial radial nerve rather than a C5–C6 trunk injury.

9. Retrieval checkpoints

Think through the answer before opening each response.

1. A patient can flex the elbow but cannot independently extend the index finger. Which posterior forearm muscle is specifically tested?

Extensor indicis, supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.

2. Wrist extension is weak and the hand has radial-deviation bias. Which extensor contributes ulnar deviation?

Extensor carpi ulnaris, attaching to metacarpal 5.

3. What forms the anatomical snuffbox borders and what artery crosses its floor?

APL/EPB lateral, EPL medial; radial artery traverses the floor over scaphoid/trapezium.

4. Why does a proximal scaphoid fragment develop avascular necrosis?

Blood enters largely distally and travels retrograde toward the proximal pole, which can lose perfusion after fracture.

5. Why does an isolated PIN lesion spare first dorsal web-space sensation?

The PIN is motor; that cutaneous sensation is carried by the superficial radial nerve.

6. What deficit is characteristic of mallet finger?

Loss of active DIP extension after disruption/avulsion of distal extensor insertion.

7. Which plexus injury causes “waiter’s tip” vs “claw hand”?

Erb-Duchenne upper (C5–C6) vs Klumpke lower (C8–T1).

Master These Before Moving On

  1. Radial branching order: High lesions can affect more muscles and cutaneous branches; distal motor branch injury need not impair sensation.
  2. Functional muscle groups: superficial vs deep; compare ECRL/ECRB/ECU with APL/EPB/EPL/extensor indicis.
  3. Snuffbox geometry: thumb tendon borders surround radial artery and scaphoid; retrograde perfusion explains proximal AVN.
  4. Skin vs root map: distinguish first web-space radial nerve from C6 thumb, C7 middle finger and C8 little finger dermatomes.
  5. Finger extensor mechanism: the dorsal expansion combines extrinsic extensor with intrinsic lumbrical/interosseous forces; distal attachment disruption causes mallet finger.

Most useful First Aid / Step 1 connections

1. Scaphoid FOOSH → snuffbox tenderness → proximal fragment ischemia. 2. Radial groove injury → wrist drop. 3. PIN motor lesion → extension deficit with spared dorsal hand sensation. 4. Upper vs lower plexus injuries → waiter’s tip vs claw hand.

Source: Morganne Manuel, “Posterior Forearm and Dorsum of the Hand,” 76-page supplied course PDF (slides and associated course handout). Enrichment is labeled where used. Some images from the lecture are retained for orientation and interpretation.
